title: Paul Graham on big startup ideas: start tiny, grow into the frightening thing
summary: Graham's 2012 keynote lists seven huge startup ideas (search, email, universities, Hollywood, a new Apple, the old Moore's law, ongoing diagnosis) and argues the biggest ideas frighten founders away. The way in is to start with a small, concrete thing a few users want, not a direct frontal attack.

principles.text: The biggest startup ideas repel you because they threaten your identity; learn to tack into that wind.
principles.quote: the biggest startup idea is threaten your identity

principles.text: Attack a giant idea by finding the tiny seed that grows into it, like a search engine used only by top hackers.
principles.quote: the way to attack all these really gigantic ideas is to find the tiny thing that turns into the gigantic idea right

principles.text: Don't announce the big ambition; build a harmless-sounding small product and let people notice the replacement later.
principles.quote: do not make a direct frontal attack on the problem don't say for example that you're going to replace email

principles.text: Really big things empirically start small and grow; founders themselves rarely know how big they'll get.
principles.quote: empirically the way to do really big things seem to be to start with small things and um grow them bigger

principles.text: Prefer a blurry view of the future to a precise one: start with something that works, then move toward the opportunity.
principles.quote: empirically it's probably better to have a blurry one

principles.text: Powerful people in pain are an opportunity: they will adopt your product first and solve your chicken-and-egg problem.
principles.quote: whenever powerful people are in pain that is an opportunity to make lots of money
